cells.tense: You are standing inside a season whose work is finished and still feeding people.
cells.act: engage the hard part on purpose and see what holds
cells.ask: Go straight at the hardest part of the commitment already costing you — not more effort, just present for that stretch.
cells.core:
What you built holds, and you can feel it holding. That's rarer than people admit. The pattern you set around the thing you've tended is carrying weight now, and you're still close enough to the ground to tell a good week from a system that works. You don't have to keep proving it. It's already load-bearing, and people stand on it without being told to.

So the next move is narrower than adding. Pick the commitment that's already asking something of you and go straight at the hard part of it this week. One friction point, on purpose. If it holds, you've learned what your commitment is made of. If it shifts, you've learned where a method was carrying the purpose instead of the other way round. Either way something unfinished gets finished, and the structure comes out simpler than it went in.
cells.sheetLine: What you tended came in, and the structure is holding.
cells.place: Where growth is given a shape others can follow

cells.tense: You are bracing for the next harvest while this one is still on the table.
cells.act: join someone in the work so the two streams run as one
cells.ask: Open a piece of what you're running to another person, and let how they do it stay in how it turns out.
cells.core:
The garden is producing, and you're already redesigning the rows. Each good result reads as proof the next one could go wrong, so the plans multiply, the structures tighten, and you're standing in the middle of abundance managing it like it's a threat. The caution is earned. The exhaustion is what it costs to keep a season from being over.

Underneath, something in you would rather build the next thing with someone than around them. Take a piece of what you're running and open it — not for a second opinion, but so the two of you run it as one. Let their approach leave a mark on the result. Two people building one structure means the design stops having to anticipate everything, and what you already grew can hold more than your own hands inside it.
cells.sheetLine: You're building the next thing before this one is finished.
cells.place: Where growth is given a shape others can follow

cells.tense: You kept the system running, and the reason you started it stayed back at the door.
cells.act: face one way for three days
cells.ask: For three days, steer everything you organize toward the outcome you'd actually want, and leave the tasks that don't serve it sitting.
cells.core:
The structure still stands, and you keep it up the way you'd keep up anything — because it's built, and stopping reads as waste. But the care has gone mechanical. You arrange whatever arrives without asking what any of it is for, and the result is a lot of parts in good order with nobody at the wheel. The abundance is still there. Your hands are still in it.

What's absent isn't effort. It's a heading. So choose one — not the sensible one, the one you'd pick if you were allowed to want something: the outcome you'd finally feel done about. For three days, aim everything you're arranging at that, and leave the rest where it lies. You'll learn fast which parts of the structure carry weight and which are just familiar. The garden doesn't need more labor. It needs to know which way it faces.
cells.sheetLine: The system runs, and you've stopped steering it.
cells.place: Where growth is given a shape others can follow

cells.tense: You designed the room other people are thriving inside and you're calling it their doing.
cells.act: drop the wrong approach and keep the commitment
cells.ask: Take a practice you keep alive out of habit, drop the form of it that's stopped working, and keep the practice.
cells.core:
People work well here. The patterns you set — how the week runs, what gets decided first, who talks to whom — are why. You'd tell anyone the results came from the team, the timing, the luck. Meanwhile you built the container they're standing in, and the story you keep about it has you off to the side, out of the frame.

Go back to your commitment, the plain form of it, before anyone handed you words for it. There's a piece of this you're carrying out of duty rather than desire. Find that piece, and release the method — not the purpose. Keep the commitment, and that version that stopped fitting can go. Underneath the duty, a choice has been running this the whole time, and the choice was yours.
cells.sheetLine: The container people stand in is one you built.
cells.place: Where growth is given a shape others can follow

attempts.check: The record does not say the person's harvest came from any particular source — family, work, or long service — so the cores describe the garden and the architecture, never who planted what. A reader could reasonably say 'the abundance isn't mine, it was the conditions' — which is exactly the misattribution the Unacknowledged cell needs, and every ask still works if the read is wrong, because each one is a single visible move, not a verdict on the person's past. The sentence that serves me more than them is any line implying they must feel proud of what grew; I've kept the cores on the structure, the pattern, and the next move instead of on a feeling they're supposed to produce.
